title: An Executive item counts as novel purely because no existing code pattern in the spell-mainnet archive covers it
content:
A.1.10.2.3.3.1 gives a one-sentence definition: "An item is considered novel if the request cannot use any of the code patterns already available in the `spell-mainnet` archive folder used on prior Spells."

Notice what the test excludes. Not financial magnitude, not political sensitivity, not how new the *idea* is — only whether an implementation precedent exists in a specific repository folder. A billion-dollar parameter change reusing a known pattern is routine; a trivial action requiring a new code path is novel and triggers the heavier process at A.1.10.2.3.3.2 (feasibility analysis, implementation proposal, two-team agreement, possible external audit) before it may even enter the Spell cadence.

The implicit risk model is that untested code, not large numbers, is what breaks Spells. Reused patterns carry the accumulated evidence of every Spell they survived; new code carries none, whatever its economic footprint.

The design payoff is that classification is nearly mechanical: two engineers can look at the archive and reach the same answer, which is why the Core Facilitator's determination at A.1.10.2.3.3.2.2 is a confirmation rather than a debate. The cost is that the archive becomes load-bearing infrastructure — its contents literally determine which governance path an item takes, so what gets committed there has consequences well beyond code reuse.
description: A.1.10.2.3.3.1 replaces judgment about importance or size with a checkable test against prior Spells, making the archive of past Spell code a governance artifact that defines process routing.
